title: Texas-Style Beef Ribs
subtitle: Massive bones, pepper crust, smoke
description: Massive bones, pepper crust, smoke. Sized for a full crew, with timing that still works when the kitchen gets interrupted.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Texas-Style Beef Ribs in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch beef. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Season the beef ribs
steps.instruction: Pull silver skin if present. Coat ribs with salt and pepper (heavy — Texas style). Let sit 30 minutes while smoker preheats to 275°F with oak.

steps.title: Smoke until tender
steps.instruction: Smoke bone-side down 6–8 hours until meat pulls back from bone and internal temp reads 200–205°F. Wrap in butcher paper if bark gets too dark before tenderness. Meat should jiggle when you shake the rack.

steps.title: Rest and portion
steps.instruction: Rest 20 minutes tented with foil. Cut between bones. Hold on sheet trays at 180°F — beef ribs dry out fast, so keep a backup pan lightly spritzed with broth.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Texas-Style Beef Ribs onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Scale for larger halls
steps.instruction: When cooking for more than 8 firefighters, split into two pans halfway through so the bottom layer does not overcook while the top waits — duplicate mise en place if you double batches.

steps.title: Serve on the line
steps.instruction: Pile ribs on sheet trays with extra pepper on the side. Backup pan in a warm oven — do not cover tightly or bark softens. Bake until the center reaches a safe internal temp (145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground) and edges look set — use a thermometer at the thickest point. Plan about 5 minutes for this step at crew scale.

steps.title: Final quality check before service
steps.instruction: Walk the line once before opening service for Texas-Style Beef Ribs — confirm hotel pans are labeled, backup trays are in the 200°F oven, and thermometers are calibrated. Rookies should ask a senior cook to spot-check the first portion.

proTips: Keep a backup tray warm in the oven for late calls — nothing worse than cold plates after a run.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Rest grilled proteins 5–8 minutes under foil before slicing — juices stay in the meat.
tonightSpread: Plate Texas-Style Beef Ribs with sides in separate pans so the crew can mix portions.
Line up Texas-Style Beef Ribs on the main counter with serving spoons — firefighters grab fast between calls.
Keep a backup tray warm in the oven at 200°F for late arrivals after a run.
Slice proteins on a cutting board at the end of the line so everyone sees the smoke ring and char.
Set sauce and pickles on the side — sauced meat holds better on the backup tray.
leftovers: Cool leftovers in shallow containers within two hours — deep pots stay hot too long.
Label trays with date and reheat to 165°F minimum before second shift.
Slice cold protein thin for next-day wraps or salads — faster reheat, less dry-out.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Massive bones, pepper crust, smoke. A hall pick for regular dinner nights — one line, real portions, no drama at the stove.

mealPrepNotes: Prep mise en place before the shift — Texas-Style Beef Ribs runs smoother when proteins are trimmed, spices are pre-measured, and hotel pans are labeled before the first tone.
